ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Loose stools after an antacid change

A 46-year-old man switches from an aluminum-containing antacid to a magnesium hydroxide preparation. Several days later he has loose stools without fever, bleeding, abdominal tenderness, or recent antibiotic exposure. Renal function is normal. Which property of the new preparation best explains the change?

  1. Destruction of intestinal villi by immune complexes
  2. Inhibition of colonic acetylcholine receptors
  3. Increased intestinal calcium absorption
  4. Osmotic retention of water by poorly absorbed magnesium salts
  5. Loss of pancreatic lipase activity from irreversible inhibition
Answer and explanation

Osmotic retention of water by poorly absorbed magnesium salts

Magnesium salts can retain water in the intestinal lumen and produce diarrhea.

Option explanations

Osmotic retention of water by poorly absorbed magnesium salts: Luminal magnesium has an osmotic laxative effect.

Loss of pancreatic lipase activity from irreversible inhibition: Magnesium hydroxide is not a pancreatic lipase inhibitor.

Destruction of intestinal villi by immune complexes: The timing and absence of inflammatory features do not suggest immune-mediated villous injury.

Inhibition of colonic acetylcholine receptors: Antimuscarinic effects tend to reduce motility rather than cause this osmotic diarrhea.

Increased intestinal calcium absorption: Calcium absorption does not explain magnesium-associated loose stools.
